content_list.content_text: The Iranian Revolution, which overthrew the Shah, Mohammad Reza Shah Pahlavi, and installed Ayatollah Khomeini as the country's supreme leader in 1979, was followed by a year of violent demonstrations. Because they were associated with the old order, film activities came to a halt. The new order brought a wave of anger against the media, which were seen as a tool of the overthrown regime. By the time the Revolution was over, 180 movie theaters had been destroyed. Over the following years, very few films were made. In 1983, the government created the Farabi Cinema Foundation, which oversaw film production and played a crucial role in ensuring that films were made within the values cherished by Islamic culture. By the end of that year, 22 feature films had already been produced.

information.contentTitle: Trailer for Through the Olive Trees
information.contentText: It is the final part of Kiarostami's Koker trilogy, and its plot revolves around the making of the second film, And Life Goes On..., which was itself a revisiting of the first film, Where Is the Friend's Home? Like much of Kiarostami's work, Through the Olive Trees is shot in a naturalistic style; a complex study of the link between art and life, its narrative often blurs the boundaries between fiction and reality. Many have since declared the film a masterpiece.

content_list.content_text: The most important filmmaker to emerge after the Revolution was Mohsen Makhmalbaf (b. 1957). A militant Muslim in the 1970s, he was imprisoned for four years under the Shah. After the Iranian Revolution, he devoted himself to cinema, having already established his reputation as a writer. Dastforoosh (The Peddler, 1989), made up of episodes exploring the plight of Iran's urban poor, brought international attention to Iranian cinema. Mohsen's work became increasingly liberal and even critical of the state.

Time of Love (1990) was banned in his home country, but, like several of his colleagues, Mohsen came to be recognized around the world as a great director for his productions: Gabbeh (1996), Nun va Goldoon (A Moment of Innocence, 1996) and Sokout (The Silence, 1998) display a lyrical visual style that captivated foreign audiences. His often rapturous approach was joined by a more urgent polemic in the powerful Safar e Ghandehar (Kandahar, 2001), about Afghan society, a film that gained even greater relevance after the September 11, 2001, attacks on the Twin Towers in New York.

information.contentText: The film won several awards, including the Golden Lion at the 2000 Venice Film Festival, but was banned in Iran.

content_list.content_text: No filmmaker has been as closely identified internationally with Iranian cinema as Abbas Kiarostami (b. 1940). His most acclaimed work of the post-Revolution years was the Koker trilogy: Khane-ye doust kodjast? (Where Is the Friend's House?, 1987), Life, and Nothing More... (1992) and Zire darakhatan zeyton (Through the Olive Trees, 1994), in which a blend of fiction and documentary erases the boundaries between the story being told and the process of its creation. The spare style of these films was refined in Ta'm e guilass (Taste of Cherry, 1997), winner of the Palme d'Or at Cannes, about a middle-aged man (Homayoun Ershadi) determined to kill himself, and Bad ma ra khahad bord (The Wind Will Carry Us, 1999), which tells the story of a clash between two worlds when an engineer from the city (Behzad Dorani) travels to a remote Kurdish village to attend the vigil of a dying woman.

quote.quote: Through the Olive Trees examines the hard work of making a film, cinema's role as a chronicler of real life, and the possibilities of love in a world where poetry and death hang symbiotically in the air.
quote.author: David Jenkins on Through the Olive Trees

content_list.content_text: The role of women became more important after the Revolution. Among the prominent female filmmakers who emerged in this period are Marzieh (b. 1969), wife of Mohsen Makhmalbaf, and his two daughters, Samira (b. 1980) and Hana (b. 1988). Marzieh wrote and directed her first film in 2000, Roozi ke zan shodam (The Day I Became a Woman, 2000), produced by her husband. It portrays three Iranian women at different stages of life: the first is a child, Hava (Fatemeh Cherag Akhar), who is declared "a woman" on her 9th birthday and is consequently required to wear a chador and forbidden to talk to boys, including her best friend; the second is a rebellious young woman, Ahoo (Shabnam Toloui), whose husband threatens her with divorce because she wants to take part in a bicycle race; and the last is a wealthy widow, Hoora (Azizeh Sedighi), who finally manages to break free from society's shackles. Marzieh then made Sag-haye velgard (Stray Dogs, 2004), a reflection on European and Hollywood cinema, and, together with her husband, directed Mardi Ke Ba Barf Amad (The Man Who Came with the Snow, 2009), a drama set in the former Soviet Union.

information.contentTitle: Trailer do filme Gosto de Cereja
information.contentText: Taste of Cherry is a minimalist film about a man who drives through the outskirts of a city in search of someone who can carry out the task of burying him after his suicide. It won the Palme d'Or at the 1997 Cannes Film Festival, which it shared with The Eel.

content_list.content_text: Samira won international acclaim for her debut film, Sib (The Apple, 1998), based on the true story of two sisters, Massoumeh and Zahra Naderi, who were kept locked up by their parents for years and then released into the world. Some critics felt the film harked back to the first native Iranian production, Khaneh siah ast (The House Is Black, 1963), a short documentary about a leper colony directed by the controversial poet Forugh Farrokhzad (1935-1967), featuring a lyrical narration by Forugh herself. The narrative structure of The Apple is more complex than that of The House Is Black, mirroring the style of Kiarostami's earlier Nema-ye Nazdik (Close-Up, 1990), in which Mohsen Makhmalbaf plays himself in a film about the case, also based on real events, of a man who tried to pass himself off as the filmmaker. Samira then directed the bold and moving Takhté siah (Blackboards, 2000), which follows the journey of a group of itinerant Kurdish teachers during the Iran-Iraq War. Panj é asr (At Five in the Afternoon, 2003) won the Jury Prize at the Cannes Film Festival and follows young Nogreh (Agheleh Rezaie) in her struggle to get an education in contemporary Afghanistan. In another self-referential cinematic twist, the making of At Five in the Afternoon in Kabul after the fall of the Taliban regime became the subject of the documentary Joy of Madness (2004), directed by Samira's sister, Hana, when she was only 14 years old.

quote.quote: The courage required to make a film like this demonstrates, resoundingly, both the gravity of the subject and the tenacity of its director.
quote.author: David Jenkins on The Circle

content_list.content_text: One of the youngest directors in world cinema, Hana has since adopted a minimalist style similar to her sister's, making Buda as Sharm Foru Rikht (Buddha Collapsed Out of Shame, 2007), about the life of Bakhtay (Nikbakht Noruz), a 5-year-old Afghan girl who lives in a cave beneath the ruins of the Buddhas of Bamiyan, destroyed by the Taliban in 2001. Her Ruzhaye Sabz (Green Days, 2009) was initially meant to be a drama about the Iranian elections of the time, but it became a semi-documentary when violence broke out after the disputed result, incorporating anonymous amateur videos.

information.contentTitle: Scenes from The Day I Became a Woman
information.contentText: Marzieh Meshkini said that, as a filmmaker, she found it particularly difficult to make a film in Iran, having to prove her abilities to the cast and crew before they accepted her.

content_list.content_text: Iran's most prominent female director is Rakhshan Bani Etemad (b. 1954). A graduate of the College of Dramatic Arts at the University of Tehran, she worked in television before directing a series of short documentaries. Etemad's first three features, Kharej az mahdudeh (Off-Limits, 1986), Zard-e ghanari (Canary Yellow, 1988) and Pul-e khareji (Foreign Currency, 1989), are close to her documentary work in their concern for the lives of society's less fortunate.

movies.title: Through the Olive Trees
movies.overview: The film focuses on one of the events in "Life, and Nothing More..." (1992), and explores the relationship between the film director, and the actors. The local actors play a couple who got married right after the earthquake. In reality, the actor is trying to persuade the actress that they should get married.
Various women struggle to function in the oppressively sexist society of contemporary Iran.
movies.title: The Circle

movies.overview: A middle-aged Tehranian man, Mr. Badii is intent on killing himself and seeks someone to bury him after his demise. Driving around the city, the seemingly well-to-do Badii meets with numerous people, including a Muslim student, asking them to take on the job, but initially he has little luck. Eventually, Badii finds a man who is up for the task because he needs the money, but his new associate soon tries to talk him out of committing suicide.
movies.title: Taste of Cherry

movies.overview: Everyday, 10-year old Khorsid takes the bus to his work at an instrument maker's shop and everyday something unexpected happens.
movies.title: The Silence
The Day I Became a Woman
movies.overview: A girl reaches the age of nine and is supposed to act as a grown woman according to her family. A girl participates in a bike race against the will of her husband. An elderly woman decides she wants to buy all the things she always wanted but could never get.

Nogreh is a young Afghani woman living with her father and her sister-in-law, Leylomah, whose husband, Akhtar, is missing. Beyond the issue of Akhtar, Leylomah is most concerned with how to feed her baby. She cannot provide milk for her baby as her own hunger is preventing her from lactating. Nogreh, however, aspires toward a life in a western styled democracy. Although the Taliban are no longer in power in Afghanistan, traditional forces are still active in the country. Nogreh often displays signs of rebellion, such as wearing a pair of white pumps instead of the traditional slipper beneath her burqa. But mostly, Nogreh wants to be educated. Without her father's knowledge, Nogreh is attending a secular girls school. Ultimately, she wants to become President of Afghanistan. With the help of a Pakistani refugee who likes her as a woman, Nogreh tries to understand exactly what forces led to current world leaders being elected, those forces which she wants to emulate.
movies.title: At Five in the Afternoon
Buddha Collapsed Out of Shame
movies.overview: A young girl zealously wants to go to school and learn to read and write. Almost everywhere she is met with hostility or indifference. The only young boy who takes her to his school is thrown out by the teacher, because helping her prevented him from arriving in time. On her way home she and other girls are taken as prisoners by boys playing as Taliban fighters. They tear her school book to pieces and threaten to stone their female captives.
